title: Your startup's A/B tests aren't scientific, they're confirmation machines
summary: Most Series A companies think they're hypothesis-driven. They're really just running confirmation bias at scale.
body_text: You ran an experiment. It was statistically significant. You shipped it. You felt scientific. You were running a confirmation machine. Here's the trap: the difference between a company that experiments and a company with an experimentation culture isn't whether you run tests. It's whether you're actually learning from them. Most Series A companies skip the learning part. They see a p-value, interpret it as permission, and move forward. That's not experimentation. That's just randomized action. The Three Stages Nobody Talks About Yuzing, who's built data and analytics at multiple high-growth startups, described three stages of experimentation maturity: Stage 1: The Gut Instinct Years No experiments at all. You're shipping based on founder intuition, customer conversations, and what you think is true. This is obviously limited. But it's honest—you know you're not being data-driven. Stage 2: The Confirmation Habit Now you run experiments. You form a hypothesis (sometimes), design a test, collect data, and ship whatever shows statistical significance. You've elevated your process. You have rigor. Except you don't. What you've actually done is systematize your confirmation bias. You're not learning faster—you're just making bad decisions feel scientific. Stage 3: Hypothesis-Driven Learning You have a hypothesis. You have success metrics. You understand what would have to be true for the experiment to matter. You run the test. You look at the results across segments and cohorts —not just the topline. You ask: who benefited? Who didn't? Does this change our thinking about how the product works? Most Series A companies believe they're at Stage 3. They're at Stage 2 and don't know it. Why Stage 2 Feels So Convincing Running a test feels rigorous. You're using statistics. You're not just guessing. And the results—when they show a winner—feel like proof. But statistical significance is not the same as a meaningful learning. Here's what actually happens at Stage 2: You form a vague hypothesis. "Increase signups." "Improve retention." Not: "Users abandon at the email confirmation step because the CTA button color doesn't contrast with our background. Changing it to high-contrast will reduce drop-off by 3%." The vague version sounds faster. It's also useless, because even if you get a winner, you don't understand why. You see a p-value and call it a decision. The experiment ran for two weeks. You hit 0.05 significance. You ship. What you don't ask: did you power the test to detect the effect size you care about? Did you calculate your sample size up front, or are you just peeking at results whenever they look good? (Airbnb found this was rampant—tests would hit significance, then converge back to nothing because the company kept peaking.) You miss that the win is asymmetric. The topline shows a 4% uplift. But you didn't cut the data by segment. What you actually found: power users see 12% uplift. New users see -2% decline. But the overall number was positive, so you shipped. Now you've solved a problem for power users and created a new one for new users. You've learned nothing. You confuse action with learning. "We ran a test. We got a winner. We shipped." That's action. Learning is: "We ran a test. We got a winner. We learned that this user segment values X, which means our onboarding assumption was wrong. Here's what we're testing next." Stage 2 looks like iteration. It's just thrashing. What Breaks at Scale The Stage 2 problem becomes obvious once you have any traffic. You can run tests fast—throw five simultaneous experiments at the wall, ship the two that hit significance. This creates the illusion of rapid learning. In reality, you're running 5 confirmations of pre-existing biases, and some of them are going to contradict the others. You end up with a product that's a patchwork of significance artifacts. Your analytics dashboard shows 47 metrics, all individually optimized, none pointing toward coherent strategy. Your founder is frustrated: "We're testing constantly but nothing seems to compound." The reason: you stopped asking "what does this teach us about our customer" and started asking "which number went up?" How to Spot if You're Stuck at Stage 2 You run a lot of tests but nothing changes. Shipping is constant. Learning is absent. The tests are tactical tweaks—button colors, copy variants, signup flow micro-optimizations. None of them connect to each other or to a larger hypothesis about product-market fit. Your experiment results rarely surprise you. If every test confirms what you already believed, you're not actually testing assumptions—you're just validating hunches with statistics. You don't segment your results. When an experiment "wins," you look at the topline. You don't break it down by user cohort, geography, feature usage, or customer segment. You have no idea if the win is broad-based or driven by a small group. Your winning experiments don't predict future behavior. You shipped the test, celebrated the win, and then... six months later, the metric drifted back. No sustained learning. No second-order effects documented. Just: we thought this would work, the test said yes, and then it didn't matter. What Stage 3 Actually Looks Like Hypothesis-driven experimentation is slow on the front end and fast on the back end. You spend time formulating a real hypothesis. Not "increase conversion" but "mobile users are converting at half the rate of desktop users because the checkout flow has unnecessary steps. Reducing the steps by two will increase mobile conversion to parity with desktop." That takes thought. It means understanding your funnel, talking to users, and making a falsifiable prediction. You design the test to actually answer the question, not just see if the metric moves. You calculate sample size up front. You decide the minimum effect size you care about. You set a stopping rule. You're not peeking. You analyze by segment. When you get results, the first thing you do is ask: "Who does this affect? What does it tell us about how people actually use this product?" A 5% topline lift that's driven entirely by users who already pay is a different insight than a 5% lift that's broad-based. You connect the result to the next experiment. You're building a chain of learning, not a collection of wins. Most importantly: you treat negative results as data, not failures. "This experiment failed" is low-resolution. "This experiment showed that our assumption about X was wrong, which means we need to rethink Y" is learning. Why This Matters to Your Growth Every company at Stage 2 believes they're running experiments. They're really running a high-powered version of gut-feel decision making, but with a p-value attached. The cost is opportunity: you're not learning what your customers actually want. You're learning what your current assumptions suggest they want. And you're reinforcing those assumptions with every test. Stage 3 costs more time up front—you have to think before you test. But the learning compounds. An experiment that teaches you something about user behavior in one part of your product informs decisions in other parts. You build a coherent product, not a random collection of optimized elements. Making the Shift Start by treating one experiment as a real learning exercise. Not five parallel tests for speed. One test, with a clear hypothesis, designed to teach you something that will change your next decision. When you get results, don't ask "did it win?" Ask "what was I wrong about, and what do I do next?" Segment your analysis. Look for where the effect is strong and where it's weak. Those edges are where the learning lives. The infrastructure matters here. If running an experiment requires three weeks and an engineer, you'll keep running Stage 2 (confirmation) because you can't afford to run Stage 3 (learning). You need a setup where you can test an idea in days, analyze the results by segment in minutes, and decide on the next test in an afternoon. At Lopus, we see teams getting stuck in this exact trap. They have dashboards, they run tests, but they're not segmenting results. A test shows a win, but they don't know if it's driven by mobile or desktop, new users or retained, free or paid. Discovery chat lets you ask "show me this test result by customer segment" in plain English — text to SQL, no analyst queue. Suddenly the win becomes a learning: where is the effect real? That question changes everything. The shift from Stage 2 to Stage 3 isn't about running more tests. It's about asking better questions. What does your current experiment culture look like? Are you seeing results that actually stick, or do they fade after you ship?

title: Presidio Production Company Announces First Quarter 2026 Results and Launch of AI-Focused Asset Intelligence Group
summary: FORT WORTH, Texas--(BUSINESS WIRE)-- Presidio Production Company (NYSE: FTW) ("Presidio" or the "Company") today announced recent highlights…...
body_text: Presidio Production Company Announces First Quarter 2026 Results and Launch of AI-Focused Asset Intelligence Group May 14, 2026 7:40pm EDT Related Documents Earnings Webcast Audio 10-Q HTML XBRL Zip FORT WORTH, Texas--(BUSINESS WIRE)-- Presidio Production Company (NYSE: FTW) ("Presidio" or the "Company") today announced recent highlights and results for the first quarter ended March 31, 2026. Recent Highlights and Outlook Closed business combination on March 4, 2026 and began trading on the New York Stock Exchange under the ticker symbol "FTW" Declared first dividend as a public company, at an equivalent rate of $1.35 per share per year Demonstrated Presidio’s acquisition strategy with Canyon Creek et al definitive purchase and sale agreements Anticipated first use of Goldman Sachs ABS Warehouse facility and dividend equivalent rate increase to $1.50 per share per year following closing of Canyon Creek acquisition Launched AI-focused Asset Intelligence Group, supported by proprietary technology at subsidiary FTW Technologies LLC Current net production of approximately 22 MBoe/d, comprising approximately 16% oil, 57% natural gas, and 27% NGLs, as of March 2026 Approximately $30 million of Adjusted EBITDA(1) expected for the second quarter of 2026 Management Commentary "The first quarter of 2026 was transformational for Presidio," said Will Ulrich, Chairman and Co-CEO. "We closed our business combination and began trading on the New York Stock Exchange on March 5. In parallel, we organized the Company around what we believe is the defining edge in our industry: Asset Intelligence, converting data into decisions, decisions into action, and action into cash flow. With our Asset Intelligence group now organized and FTW Technologies operating as a dedicated business unit, we are targeting a three to five percent production uplift in 2026 across our existing asset base. We have already achieved approximately one percent of production uplift through April. Over time, we believe the intellectual property we are building at FTW Technologies has applications well beyond our own acreage and represents an additional source of value for shareholders." Chris Hammack, Co-CEO, added: "Acquisitions are the engine of our growth model, and we believe the Canyon Creek transaction is the first proof point of that strategy as a public company. Canyon Creek will extend our footprint into the Arkoma Basin, expands our producing base alongside our existing Mid-Continent assets. Land-and-expand remains the strategy, and the pipeline for acquisitions has never been deeper." First Quarter Results First quarter results are bifurcated into a predecessor period and a successor period reflecting the new basis of accounting established at the closing of the business combination on March 4, 2026. The first quarter included transaction-related charges associated with closing, including transaction costs, non-cash stock-based compensation, and other one-time items which significantly impacted net income (loss). In addition, the Company executed a restructuring of its commodity hedge book concurrent with closing; the restructuring resulted in $2.2 million of realized derivative costs recognized in the successor period, whereas the economic benefit of the restructured hedges began in the second quarter of 2026. As a result, both the predecessor and successor periods reflect transaction-driven items and pre-restrike hedge economics that management does not expect to have a recurring impact on future (or forecasted) performance. Accordingly, management is providing guidance that it expects approximately $30 million of Adjusted EBITDA(1) for the second quarter of 2026. AI and Asset Intelligence Presidio applies a disciplined, data-driven playbook to modernize acquired oilfield operations. The Company transforms oil and gas assets into high-efficiency operations through repeatable systems and empowered field execution. The latest evolution of this efficiency is focused on the implementation of AI. As such, Presidio has launched the organization of its operations into three integrated functions: an Asset Intelligence group of engineers and support staff with AI and analytics to drive field efficiencies; an Operations group running the assets day-to-day; and dedicated AI development at subsidiary FTW Technologies that builds tools, models, and insights the Asset Intelligence group uses to make better decisions faster. The Company also designated its first class of Presidio AI Astronauts, employees serving as internal ambassadors of the AI transformation across the organization. The Asset Intelligence group carries a target of three to five percent production growth in 2026 across Presidio's existing asset base. Through the first four months of 2026, the Company has achieved an approximately one percent production uplift. The Company's technology platform is operated by FTW Technologies LLC, a wholly owned subsidiary. FTW Technologies has built a proprietary oil and gas domain model built on a custom ontology and trained on years of operating data, including voice submissions from field pumpers, well files, drilling, completion, and workover reports, producing pressures, production volumes, and geology to surface well-level decisions in real time. Presidio is expanding its dedicated AI team. The Company believes the intellectual property developed at FTW Technologies has applications beyond Presidio's own assets and represents a potential additional source of value to shareholders over time. Acquisition Outlook With the global rise in commodity prices, the Company has observed an increase in A&D activity and currently has $1.4 billion of bids in process across multiple potential transactions. The Company’s expected acquisition outlook remains strong. On May 8, 2026, the Company executed definitive purchase and sale agreements to acquire the Canyon Creek assets from companies controlled by Vortus Investments and additional sellers for approximately $83 million in aggregate consideration, comprising $60.0 million of cash and 2,173,913 shares of Presidio common stock issued to the sellers. The cash portion is expected to be funded through borrowings under the Company's planned $1.0 billion Goldman Sachs ABS Warehouse Facility and cash on hand. The transaction follows the letter of intent announced February 24, 2026, and is expected to close in the third quarter of 2026, subject to customary closing conditions and post-closing adjustments. Upon closing, Canyon Creek will represent the Company's first completed acquisition as a public company and demonstrates the Company’s acquisition thesis. The Canyon Creek assets establish the Company's entry into the Arkoma Basin, an operationally adjacent extension of the existing Mid-Continent footprint and a platform for further consolidation consistent with the Company's land-and-expand strategy. The acquired position comprises 55 active producing wells generating approximately 21.4 MMcfe/d of net PDP production as of April 2026, weighted approximately 70% to natural gas and 30% to natural gas liquids, with an estimated base decline of approximately 11% per year. Management estimates net PDP reserves of approximately 100 Bcfe and PV-10 of approximately $100 million. The Company expects the incremental cash flow from Canyon Creek to support an increase in the anticipated annualized dividend from $1.35 to $1.50 per share following close, subject to approval by the Board of Directors. Liquidity and Capital Structure As of March 31, 2026, Presidio had total liquidity of $48.7 million, comprising $20.7 million of unrestricted cash and cash equivalents and $28.0 million of undrawn capacity under its revolving credit facility ("RBL"). Total cash and cash equivalents was $31.5 million, including restricted cash of $10.8 million. Indebtedness consisted of $256.8 million of investment grade asset-backed security ("ABS") notes, $37.0 million of RBL borrowings, and a $2.1 million Trail Dust term loan, for total Net Debt of $264.4 million(1)(2). Based on approximately $30 million of Adjusted EBITDA(1) expected for the second quarter of 2026, this equates to Leverage(1) of approximately 2.2x on a second-quarter annualized basis, using debt balances as of March 31, 2026. Preferred equity outstanding consisted of Series A preferred stock with a $125.0 million aggregate stated value and Series B preferred stock convertible into 2,717,300 shares (3). Common equity outstanding consisted of 27,652,068 shares of Class A Common Stock and 1,676,830 shares of Class B Common Stock. About Presidio Production Company Headquartered in Fort Worth, TX, Presidio Production Company (NYSE: FTW) is a yield-focused, differentiated oil and gas operator in the United States focused on the acquisition and optimization of producing oil and natural gas wells, without drilling. Presidio is a leading operator of stable oil and gas wells across the Mid-Continent, applying engineering expertise and AI-driven analytics to enhance performance and extend asset life. The Company's Class A common stock is listed on the New York Stock Exchange under the ticker symbol "FTW". To learn more, visit https://bypresidio.com/ . Non-GAAP Financial Measures and Reconciliations This press release includes Adjusted EBITDA and Adjusted Unhedged EBITDA, which are financial measures not calculated in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles in the United States ("GAAP"). Presidio defines Adjusted EBITDA as net income (loss) before (1) interest expense, net, (2) depreciation, depletion, amortization and accretion, (3) unrealized loss (gain) on derivative instruments, (4) non-cash share-based compensation, (5) non-recurring compensation expense related to our Class B Units, (6) (gain) loss on sale of assets, net, (7) loss on ARO liabilities, (8) change in fair value of earnout liability, (9) income tax expense (benefit), and (10) acquisition, transaction, and certain non-recurring costs that management does not consider indicative of ongoing performance. Adjusted EBITDA is used as a supplemental financial performance measure by Presidio management and by external users of our financial statements, such as industry analysts, investors, lenders, rating agencies and others, to evaluate our operating performance and Presidio’s results of operations from period to period and against our peers without regard to financing methods, capital structure or historical cost basis. We exclude the items listed above from net income (loss) in arriving at Adjusted EBITDA because these items and related amounts can vary substantially from company to company within our industry depending upon accounting methods and book values of assets, capital structures and the method by which the assets were acquired. Adjusted EBITDA is not a measurement of our financial performance under GAAP and should not be considered as an alternative to, or more meaningful than, net income (loss) as determined in accordance with GAAP or as an indicator of our operating performance. Certain items excluded from Adjusted EBITDA are significant components in understanding and assessing a company’s financial performance, such as a company’s cost of capital and tax burden, as well as the historic costs of depreciable assets, none of which are reflected in Adjusted EBITDA. Our presentation of Adjusted EBITDA should not be construed as an inference that our results will be unaffected by unusual items. Our computations of Adjusted EBITDA may not be identical to other similarly titled measures of other companies. Presidio defines Adjusted Unhedged EBITDA as Adjusted EBITDA further adjusted to remove realized gains and losses on derivative instruments. This measure is intended to show our operating results without the impact of our hedging program. Management believes Adjusted Unhedged EBITDA is an important metric that provides valuable insight into the Company’s underlying operational performance by removing the effects of financing decisions, non-cash charges, and hedging activities. Adjusted Unhedged EBITDA is a supplemental non-GAAP measure and may not be comparable to similarly titled measures of other companies. Adjusted EBITDA and Adjusted Unhedged EBITDA are not substitutes for, and should be considered in addition to, net income (loss), cash flows from operating activities, or any other measure of financial performance or liquidity presented in accordance with GAAP. Adjusted EBITDA and Adjusted Unhedged EBITDA as presented may not be comparable to similarly titled measures of other companies. A reconciliation of Adjusted EBITDA and Adjusted Unhedged EBITDA to net loss, the most directly comparable GAAP measure, is provided below. Presidio defines Net Debt as the aggregate principal amount outstanding of the Company’s ABS notes, RBL borrowings and Trail Dust term loan, excluding lease obligations, less total cash (including restricted cash). Presidio defines Leverage as Net Debt divided by annualized Adjusted EBITDA, calculated by multiplying the applicable quarter’s Adjusted EBITDA by four. Management believes Net Debt and Leverage are useful to investors, analysts and rating agencies in evaluating the Company’s capital structure and ability to service its indebtedness. Net Debt and Leverage are supplemental non-GAAP measures, should not be considered alternatives to total debt or net income (loss) determined in accordance with GAAP, and may not be comparable to similarly titled measures of other companies. A reconciliation of Net Debt to total debt, the most directly comparable GAAP measure, is set forth below. The Leverage ratio presented in this press release is calculated using forward-looking Adjusted EBITDA for the second quarter of 2026. The Company is unable to provide a reconciliation of forward-looking Adjusted EBITDA to forward-looking net loss, the most directly comparable GAAP measure, without unreasonable effort because certain reconciling items, including unrealized gains and losses on derivative instruments, income tax expense (benefit), and the timing and amount of acquisition, transaction and other non-recurring costs, depend on future events outside the Company’s control or cannot be reasonably predicted. The PV-10 present in this press release is a non-GAAP financial measure that represents the present value of estimated future cash inflows from proved oil and gas reserves, less future development and production costs, discounted at 10% per annum to reflect the timing of future cash flows and utilizes an SEC pricing assumption. PV-10 is derived from the standardized measure of discounted future net cash flows (the “Standardized Measure”), which is the most directly comparable financial measure calculated in accordance with GAAP. PV-10 differs from the Standardized Measure in that PV-10 excludes the effects of income taxes on future net revenues. We believe the presentation of PV-10 is relevant and useful to investors because it provides the discounted future net cash flows attributable to our proved reserves without regard to any of our specific income tax characteristics and is a useful measure for evaluating the relative monetary significance of our oil and natural gas properties. Investors may use PV-10 as a basis for comparing the relative size and value of our proved reserves to that of other companies. PV-10 should not be considered as a substitute for, or more meaningful than, the Standardized Measure. Neither PV-10 nor the Standardized Measure represents an estimate of the fair market value of our oil and natural gas properties. title: How Ferguson Outgrew the British Company That Bought It
summary: Ferguson tops MDM's 2025 Plumbing list at No. 1. The stranger story: it grew big enough to rename, then shed, the UK parent that once owned it.
body_text: Part of Distributor Playbooks — strategy teardowns of every company on the 2025 MDM Top Distributors lists . Ferguson opens 2025 at No. 1 on MDM's Top Distributors list for Plumbing, with a No. 2 finish in PVF and HVACR and top-12 placements across Industrial Supplies, MRO, Building Materials and JanSan. MDM credits the company with $29.6 billion in 2024 revenue, roughly 35,000 employees and about 1,800 locations. That scale is the least interesting thing about Ferguson. The stranger story is how a Newport News, Virginia plumbing supply house ended up owning the name of the British conglomerate that bought it. A Virginia plumbing shop, bought and swallowed Charles Ferguson, Ralph Lenz and Johnny Smither started Ferguson Enterprises in Newport News in 1953 as a plumbing and heating distributor. Growth was steady rather than spectacular for two decades, then in 1982 the company was acquired by Wolseley plc , a UK building-materials conglomerate, for $30.7 million. On paper that was the end of Ferguson as an independent story: an American plumbing wholesaler folded into a much larger British parent. It didn't play out that way. Ferguson kept growing inside Wolseley's portfolio, expanded into new US regions, and merged with Familian Corporation of Los Angeles in 1999 to push further west. By the 2010s the US plumbing and HVAC business wasn't just Wolseley's biggest division, it was effectively the company. In 2017 Wolseley plc changed its own corporate name to Ferguson plc, an unusual move: the acquired subsidiary's brand replaced the acquiring parent's identity on the London Stock Exchange ticker. The insight: the subsidiary became the parent, then went home That renaming is the hinge of Ferguson's story, and it is worth stating plainly because it is easy to miss on the company's own history page: most distributors that get bought by a bigger conglomerate stay divisions. Ferguson became the whole company. It didn't stop there. In January 2021, Ferguson divested its remaining UK retail operations to private equity firm Clayton, Dubilier & Rice for £308 million, cutting the last operating tie to the country its parent came from. That same year it shifted its primary stock listing to the New York Stock Exchange. By August 2023 it qualified as a US domestic filer under SEC rules, and in August 2024 it completed a full corporate reorganization, replacing Ferguson plc with a new Delaware parent, Ferguson Enterprises Inc. , while the old Jersey-incorporated entity was renamed and quietly wound down to a shell. Forty-two years after a British company bought a Virginia plumbing wholesaler, the wholesaler finished the trade: it kept the growth, took the name, and sent the foreign incorporation home. Few companies in distribution have a founding story that ends with them out-lasting and out-scaling their own acquirer this cleanly. Year Event 1953 Ferguson Enterprises founded in Newport News, VA 1982 Acquired by Wolseley plc (UK) for $30.7M 1999 Merges with Familian Corporation, expands to the West Coast 2017 Wolseley plc renamed itself Ferguson plc 2021 Divests UK operations to CD&R; primary listing moves to NYSE 2023 Qualifies as a US domestic filer 2024 Redomiciles as Ferguson Enterprises Inc., a Delaware corporation What the machine looks like today Underneath the corporate history is a distribution business built on density and specialization. Ferguson runs nearly 1,700 to 1,800 branches (the figure moves with each quarterly close) plus more than 270 high-end showrooms that sell fixtures directly to homeowners and designers, feeding a separate residential channel alongside its core wholesale trade counter business. About 5,000 outside sales reps call on contractors and job sites; a further 5,000-plus associates run national accounts. Digital has become a real second leg rather than a defense against Amazon: digital orders grew 28% year over year to reach 46% of pro sales in fiscal 2024, and Ferguson has been consolidating its e-commerce identity, merging its Build.com consumer brand into the main Ferguson site in 2025. The other constant is acquisitions. Ferguson has done roughly 50 deals over the past five years and closed fiscal 2025 with nine of them in specialty categories like waterworks, environmental products and duct supply, adding about $300 million in annualized revenue. MDM put full fiscal 2025 sales at $31.3 billion , up 5% on the year, with acquisitions contributing a modest but steady one point of growth and non-residential construction driving the rest. The tension worth naming Ferguson is buying and pruning at the same time, and both are visible in the same fiscal year. While closing nine tuck-in deals, the company also recorded $14 million in restructuring charges tied to branch closures in Canada and sold a shuttered US distribution center. That is not contradiction so much as discipline: a company this size can add specialty capability through M&A in one region while rationalizing underperforming footprint in another, and treat both as normal maintenance rather than crisis. The risk sits in the mix, not the mechanics. Ferguson's growth is now split between an M&A engine that adds a point of revenue a year and a non-residential construction cycle that can swing much harder than that, and the model has to keep both moving in the same direction to keep compounding at this rate. The Plumbing #1 ranking MDM hands Ferguson each year measures the branches, the trucks and the revenue. It doesn't capture the part of the story that is actually unusual: a company that grew past the parent that bought it, took its name, and then went and got its own address back.

title: Shopify vs Etsy: Which Platform Is Better for Your Online Business in 2026?
summary: When comparing Shopify vs Etsy, e-commerce sellers are not simply choosing between two places to list their products online.
body_text: Form Your LLC Today. Foreign Founders Welcome. Get Started for Free E-commerce Shopify vs Etsy: Which Platform Is Better for Your Online Business in 2026? By Karishma Borkakoty Published on 28 May 2026 21 min read When comparing Shopify vs Etsy, e-commerce sellers are not simply choosing between two places to list their products online. They are choosing between two different business models. Etsy is a marketplace. It gives sellers access to an existing buyer base, marketplace discovery, and a standardized selling environment. Shopify is an e-commerce platform for building an independent store. It gives sellers control over their storefront, branding, customer experience, and business systems. That difference matters because it affects far more than setup. It influences how you acquire customers, how much control you have over pricing and brand presentation, how repeat purchases happen, and how the business scales over time. So, it’s not just Shopify vs Etsy . It is whether you want to plug into existing demand or build an asset you actually own. This matters even more in 2026, when customer acquisition is more expensive, marketplace competition is harsher, and serious operators care a lot more about first-party customer relationships than they did a few years ago. If you are trying to decide between the two, this guide will help you pick the best platform based on cost structure, setup friction, traffic model, branding control, SEO upside, and long-term growth. Let’s quickly get to it. Shopify vs Etsy: Quick Comparison Feature Shopify (Your Own Store) Etsy (Marketplace) Best For Scaling brands & repeat customers Niche, handmade, & first-time sales Upfront Cost $39/mo (Basic) or $29/mo (Annual) $0/mo ($15 setup fee for new shops) Transaction Fees 0% (with Shopify Payments) 6.5% of total order (inc. shipping) Listing Fees None (Unlimited products) $0.20 per item (expires every 4 months) Payment Proc. 2.9% + $0.30 (US Basic) 3% + $0.25 (US) Traffic Source You (SEO, Social, Ads, Email) Etsy (Internal search & “Offsite Ads”) Data Ownership Full (You own your email list) Limited (Etsy owns the customer data) Design Freedom Total (800+ themes, custom CSS) Restricted (Standard Etsy layout) The 2026 “Value Triggers” The “Break-Even” Revenue: Mathematical data shows that once your shop consistently clears $1,500 – $2,000 in monthly sales , Shopify becomes cheaper. At this volume, Etsy’s 6.5% transaction fee plus listing renewals usually costs more than Shopify’s $39 fixed monthly fee. The Marketplace Risk: Etsy’s “Offsite Ads” are often mandatory for shops earning over $10k/year. This adds an additional 12% fee to sales Etsy attributes to their advertising, which can instantly evaporate the margins of low-priced goods. The Search Reality: On Etsy, you are one click away from a competitor’s “Similar Item” being recommended at the bottom of your own page. On Shopify, the only products the customer sees are yours. Decision Hack: If you’re just testing a hobby, start on Etsy . If you have a business plan and a marketing strategy (Instagram, TikTok, or Email), go Shopify from Day 1 to avoid the headache of migrating your data later. What Is Shopify? Screenshot Shopify is a comprehensive e-commerce platform that acts as the “operating system” for your independent business. Unlike a marketplace, it gives you a dedicated domain name and a standalone website. In 2026, it is no longer just a site builder; it is a multi-channel hub that syncs your inventory across TikTok, Instagram, Amazon, and even physical Point-of-Sale (POS) locations. Key Features Shopify Store Setup: A streamlined onboarding process that uses “Online Store 2.0” technology, allowing you to build a high-converting site using modular blocks rather than complex code. Shopify Payments: An integrated checkout system that supports everything from credit cards to “Buy Now, Pay Later” (BNPL) and crypto, without requiring third-party plugins. App Ecosystem: A massive library of tools for SEO, automated shipping, and AI-driven customer service. Global Scaling: Built-in tools for “Markets” that automatically localize currencies, languages, and duties for international buyers. Best For Ambitious Scaling: Businesses that want to grow from their first sale to $1M+ without switching platforms. Brand Builders: Entrepreneurs who want total control over their customer’s experience, from the landing page to the post-purchase thank-you email. Multichannel Sellers: Anyone selling through a mix of social media, brick-and-mortar, and a standalone website. Data-Driven Owners: Those who want to own their customer data and email lists to drive repeat sales, something not possible on marketplace-only platforms. 🔖 Learn more: Shopify Requirements for US and Non-US Sellers What Is Etsy? Screenshot Etsy is a global marketplace that has spent over two decades carving out a specific niche in the e-commerce world. It isn’t just another site to buy stuff; it’s a dedicated ecosystem for three distinct categories: Handmade goods, Vintage items (at least 20 years old), and Craft supplies. The platform has evolved into a sophisticated “plug-and-play” solution. When you start selling on Etsy marketplace , you aren’t just getting a storefront, you’re buying into a massive, pre-built audience of over 450 million monthly visitors. Key Features Built-in Traffic & Discovery: The biggest draw of the Etsy marketplace is its internal search engine. Unlike a standalone site where you have to hunt for every visitor, Etsy’s algorithm actively connects your products with high-intent buyers already searching for unique, personalized items. AI-Driven Search (2026 Update): Etsy has overhauled its search to prioritize “natural language.” The algorithm now understands the context behind a search (like “minimalist anniversary gift for him”) rather than just matching repetitive keywords, rewarding sellers who write clear, human-focused descriptions. The Star Seller Badge: This is Etsy’s “seal of approval.” By maintaining a 95% response rate and 95% on-time shipping, you earn a badge that signals instant trust to shoppers, often leading to higher conversion rates in a crowded market. Stable Listing URLs: A recent technical update ensures that your listing links remain permanent even if you edit them. This makes selling on Etsy much more effective for long-term SEO, as Google can now index your products more reliably without broken links. Integrated Marketing Tools: From “Offsite Ads” (where Etsy pays to advertise your products on Google and Instagram) to internal “Etsy Ads,” the platform gives you a tiered way to scale your visibility based on your budget. Best For Solopreneurs and Hobbyists: If you want to go from “idea” to “first sale” in a single afternoon without worrying about web design or hosting, Etsy should be your choice. Niche Artisans: Makers who produce highly specific, specialized items that benefit from a community that values “unique” over “mass-produced.” Proof-of-Concept: Entrepreneurs who want to test if a product will actually sell before investing the time and money into a full Shopify store setup. Low-Volume, High-Margin Sellers: Because of the $0.20 listing fee and 6.5% transaction fee, Etsy is perfect for those who sell fewer, higher-priced items where they don’t mind a “pay-as-you-go” cost structure. 🔖 Learn more: How to Sell on Etsy in 6 Steps Shopify vs Etsy: Ease of Use and Setup If you’re looking for the path of least resistance, Etsy is the clear winner for getting an item live fast. The setup is essentially a series of forms; you upload a photo, write a description, set a price, and you are officially “in business.” Because Etsy is a standardized marketplace, you aren’t responsible for designing the architecture of the shop, you are simply moving into a pre-built website. This makes Shopify vs Etsy for beginners a lopsided debate if the only metric is speed. Etsy handles the hosting, the SSL certificates, and the mobile optimization by default, meaning a novice can bypass the steep learning curve of web design entirely. However, that speed comes at the cost of ownership. Shopify demands a greater time investment upfront to build and customize your own dedicated e-commerce website . This effort, however, provides you with complete ownership and control, allowing you to create a unique, branded, and fully customizable customer experience. While Shopify’s modern drag-and-drop editor is incredibly intuitive, you are still the one making the creative calls. This extra effort is precisely what builds a stronger foundation. The best choice depends on your goal: Select Etsy if your priority is speed and product validation; choose Shopify if your goal is to establish a long-term, scalable, and fully owned brand. Shopify vs Etsy: Fees When people compare Shopify vs Etsy fees , they usually make one mistake: they look only at the starting cost, not at what happens to profit as the business grows. In 2026, the fee structures for both platforms have diverged significantly, moving toward a “pay-as-you-go” marketplace model versus a “fixed-cost” infrastructure model. The Marketplace Tax: Decoding Etsy’s Costs Etsy is viable because of its low barrier to entry, but as you scale, those “small” percentages can begin to bite. Every item you list costs $0.20 (expiring every four months), which is negligible for a few products but adds up for large catalogs. The real weight, however, is the 6.5% transaction fee applied to the total order value, including the shipping you charge the customer. When you add the standard 3% + $0.25 payment processing fee (for US sellers), you’re already losing nearly 10% of every sale. The “silent margin killer” on Etsy is the mandatory Offsite Ads program. If you cross $10,000 in annual revenue, Etsy automatically advertises your products across the web. If a sale comes from one of those clicks, they take an additional 12% fee (15% for smaller shops). In a worst-case scenario, between transaction, processing, and offsite ad fees, Etsy can consume over 20-25% of a single sale’s revenue. The Infrastructure Investment: Shopify’s Fixed Fees Shopify charges a monthly subscription fee, like paying rent for your store’s platform, regardless of how much you sell. The Basic plan is $39/month (or $29 if you pay for a year). The good news is that if you use Shopify’s own payment system (Shopify Payments), they don’t charge a separate transaction fee. You only pay the standard credit card processing rate, which starts at 2.9% plus 30 cents per transaction. While there are no fees to list products, be aware of extra costs for add-on apps. Most serious sellers spend an additional $20 to $100 monthly on specialized apps for things like better search engine optimization (SEO), customer loyalty programs, or suggesting related products (upsells). The Break-Even Realities To understand how Shopify vs Etsy fees affect your business, think about how much you sell each month: Selling a little (less than $1,300/month): Etsy is cheaper. If you only make about $500 in sales, your total fees on Etsy would be around $52, but Shopify would cost you almost $100 (due to its monthly fee plus processing costs). The tipping point (around $1,350/month): This is the break-even point. Once you sell more than this, Etsy’s 6.5% sales fee (the “success tax”) starts to cost more than Shopify’s fixed monthly subscription (around $39). Selling a lot ($10,000+/month): Shopify is the clear winner here. For $10,000 in sales, Etsy might take over $1,000 in fees. With Shopify, your total costs, even with extra paid tools, would likely be closer to $400–$500. The main difference: Etsy has variable costs , which is great when sales are slow because you don’t pay much. Shopify has fixed costs , which rewards you as your business grows because the fixed fee stays the same. If you plan to keep your business small, stay on Etsy; if you want to grow into a major brand, Shopify’s subscription model will save you money. Shopify vs Etsy: Traffic and Customer Acquisition The fundamental difference between these two platforms lies in who holds the keys to the audience. Here is a simplified explanation of the traffic and customer acquisition difference between Shopify and Etsy: Etsy (The Digital Department Store): Traffic: Etsy already has a massive audience, it’s like a crowded department store. Buyers come directly to Etsy looking for unique products. Customer Acquisition: You don’t have to find customers; Etsy’s search engine and tools do the work of showing your product to interested shoppers. You can get your first sale fast without paying for external ads. The Trade-off: The customers belong to Etsy. You can’t easily market to them later, and you are always dependent on Etsy’s rules and algorithms. This is “borrowed” traffic. Shopify (Your Own Standalone Store): Traffic: Shopify gives you a powerful website, but it starts with zero visitors. It’s an empty store you built on a quiet street. Customer Acquisition: You are 100% responsible for bringing in every customer through advertising (Google Ads, Facebook, etc.) and other methods (SEO, social media). The Trade-off: While getting traffic is harder and costs more upfront, you own the customer data (email, phone number). This allows you to drive repeat sales cheaply through email or text, improving your long-term profits. This is “owned” traffic. The key takeaway: Ultimately, the choice between Etsy traffic vs Shopify traffic is a trade-off between immediate traction and long-term scalability. Etsy is the superior laboratory for testing product-market fit because it eliminates the friction of finding an audience. However, as a business matures, the reliance on a third-party algorithm becomes a liability. Shopify allows you to move away from the model where you constantly rely on “pay-per-click” or “percentage-per-sale” fees. Instead, it enables you to build a valuable, self-sustaining business asset where your own brand, not the marketplace platform, becomes the main driver of your growth. Shopify vs Etsy: Branding and Customization Branding and customization are not small differences between these two platforms. They directly affect how customers perceive your business and whether they remember your brand or just the platform where they bought the product. On Etsy, your store exists within a standard marketplace format. The layout, product display, and overall shopping experience follow Etsy’s structure, so there is only limited room to make your store feel distinct. You can add your logo, banner, shop announcement, and product photography, but the overall environment still feels like Etsy. Customers are often comparing your listing with similar products on the same page, which makes differentiation harder. In many cases, the buyer remembers that they purchased something on Etsy, but not necessarily which brand they purchased it from. Shopify gives you much more control over how your business is presented. You can customize your homepage, product pages, navigation, colors, fonts, collections, checkout experience, and brand messaging. That matters because strong branding does more than make a store look attractive. It helps create trust, supports premium pricing, and gives customers a reason to come back to your website instead of searching for similar products again. To sum it up, Etsy helps you sell within an existing marketplace, while Shopify helps you build a branded business that customers can recognize, remember, and return to directly. Shopify vs Etsy: SEO and Discoverability When you compare Etsy vs Shopify SEO , the difference is structural, not just technical. Both platforms help you get discovered, but they do it in completely different ways, and that directly affects how much control you have over your traffic. On Etsy, SEO happens inside the marketplace. Etsy’s own search system works in two stages: first, it matches listings to a buyer’s query using elements like titles, tags, categories, and attributes. Next, it ranks those listings based on performance signals like clicks, conversions, reviews, and overall shop quality . In 2026, this system is even more behavior-driven. Listings that earn engagement and sales get pushed higher, which means your visibility depends not just on keywords but on how well your product performs once seen . This makes Etsy SEO relatively faster to work with. You don’t need domain authority or backlinks. If your listing matches buyer intent and performs well, it can start getting visibility within the marketplace quickly. But the limitation is clear: your traffic is tied to Etsy’s ecosystem. You are optimizing for Etsy’s algorithm, not building independent search presence. Shopify works very differently. There is no built-in marketplace search pushing your products. Instead, SEO is focused on ranking your own website on search engines like Google. Shopify gives you control over key elements like meta titles, URLs, structured data, and content through blogs and landing pages, which allows you to build long-term organic visibility . But unlike Etsy, this takes time. Search engines evaluate authority, relevance, and content depth before sending consistent traffic. The core difference comes down to control. Etsy helps you get discovered faster within a closed system. Shopify allows you to build discoverability that exists outside any platform. One is optimized for immediate visibility, the other for long-term traffic ownership. Shopify vs Etsy: Payment Options and Checkout Experience The difference here comes down to how much control you want over payments and what kind of checkout experience you’re willing to accept. Etsy is designed for simplicity. Shopify is designed for flexibility. How payments work on Etsy Etsy uses a system called Etsy Payments , which is mandatory for most sellers. It supports major payment methods like credit/debit cards, PayPal (in many regions) , Apple Pay, Google Pay, and Etsy gift cards. Here are some core features of Etsy Payments: Etsy manages the entire checkout flow Buyers stay within the Etsy platform from discovery to payment Currency conversion and local payment methods are handled by Etsy Funds are deposited into your account based on Etsy’s payout schedule This makes checkout very smooth for buyers, especially because many of them already trust Etsy and have used it before. But there are limitations. For example: You cannot customize the checkout experience You cannot add upsells, bundles, or post-purchase offers Customer data access is limited compared to independent stores You are dependent on Etsy’s payment policies and timelines In short, Etsy optimizes for convenience, but removes control. How Payments Work On Shopify Shopify gives you significantly more flexibility . Its native system, Shopify Payments, supports major cards, Apple Pay, Google Pay, Shop Pay, and in many regions, local payment methods. For example: You can use Shopify Payments or integrate third-party gateways (Stripe, PayPal, Razorpay, etc.) You can sell in multiple currencies and enable localized checkout experiences Checkout can be optimized with features like discount codes, bundles, subscriptions, and upsells Shop Pay (Shopify’s accelerated checkout) is widely used and designed to improve conversion rates Shopify gives you much more control over the payment experience, which becomes important as your store grows. You can tailor checkout more closely to your brand, introduce post-purchase upsells and cross-sells to increase order value, and connect tools for subscriptions, bundles, or one-click add-ons. More importantly, the entire journey, from product discovery to final payment happens within your own store environment, which gives you greater control over conversion, customer experience, and retention. The key takeaway: Etsy prioritizes ease and trust within its marketplace. Shopify prioritizes control, flexibility, and revenue optimization as your business grows. Shopify vs Etsy: Scalability and Business Growth The gap between Etsy and Shopify becomes much clearer once your business starts growing. In the early stage, Etsy can help you get traction faster. But once you begin thinking about margins, repeat customers, brand control, and expansion, the platform starts to feel more limiting. Why Etsy works in the early stage Etsy can be effective when you are still validating demand. It gives you: Access to built-in marketplace traffic A lower barrier to entry A faster route to first sales That makes it useful for testing products, especially in categories where Etsy already has strong buyer intent. Where Etsy starts to become limiting As sales volume increases, Etsy’s structure becomes harder to grow with. The main limitations are: Fees rise as revenue rises, which puts pressure on margins Your products sit next to competing listings, making price comparison easy Branding remains limited You do not fully own the customer relationship This means growth can happen, but it happens inside Etsy’s system, not fully on your terms. Why businesses move to Shopify Shopify is better suited for businesses that want to scale with more control. It gives you the ability to: Keep platform costs more predictable as revenue grows Build email marketing and retention flows Segment customers and drive repeat purchases Expand across your own site, social channels, and other sales channels Create a stronger brand that customers remember directly The core difference: Etsy helps you get discovered. Shopify helps you build systems. That is why major businesses often start on Etsy but eventually move to Shopify, or make Shopify their primary store. Etsy can support early traction, but Shopify gives you the structure needed for sustainable, long-term growth. Shopify vs Etsy: Pros and Cons Before you decide, you need to look at these platforms from a business lens, not a feature list. The difference between these platforms can affect margins, control, and how far you can actually grow. One is a high-yield infrastructure ; the other is a high-traffic marketplace . So, let’s understand a few core pros and cons of both the platforms. Factor Shopify (Owned Infrastructure) Etsy (Global Marketplace) Business Model Independent store (you own the platform experience) Marketplace (you operate within Etsy’s ecosystem) Primary Traffic Outbound: You generate traffic (ads, SEO, social) Inbound: Etsy’s search engine delivers active buyers to you. Built-in marketplace traffic. Cost Structure Fixed Heavy: High monthly sub ($39) but low per-sale tax. Variable Heavy: $0 monthly sub but high ~10–25% per-sale tax. Customer Data Full Ownership: You own the email/SMS list for life. Rented: Etsy owns the customer; remarketing is restricted. Branding Limitless. Custom UX/UI, checkout, and packaging. Full control over design and experience. Limited, standardized storefront Scalability Infinite. High, supports multi-channel growth. Capped. Fees scale linearly with your success (6.5% + ads). Limited by marketplace structure. Risk Factor Low platform dependency. High dependency on Etsy policies/algorithm. One algorithm change can kill your traffic. Shopify Pros Shopify gives you control where it actually matters. You control pricing, customer experience, and how your brand is perceived. As your revenue increases, your costs don’t scale in the same way, which protects margins. More importantly, you can build systems around your business, email marketing, retention, upsells, and repeat purchase flows. This is what turns a store into a business. Shopify Cons The biggest drawback is that nothing is handed to you. You have to generate your own traffic, which means investing time or money into marketing. There is also an upfront commitment with monthly fees and initial setup effort. If you’re not ready to think about branding and acquisition, Shopify can feel slow at the start. Etsy Pros Etsy removes friction in the early stage. You get access to a large, intent-driven audience without spending on ads. Setup is fast, and you can start selling almost immediately. For testing products or running a side hustle, this makes it one of the easiest entry points into e-commerce. Etsy Cons The limitations show up as you grow. Fees increase with every sale, which eats into margins. Your products are displayed next to competitors, making differentiation harder. Branding is limited, and you don’t fully control the customer relationship. There is also platform risk, changes in Etsy’s algorithm or policies can directly impact your sales. Shopify vs Etsy: Which One Should You Choose? This decision becomes much clearer when you tie it to your stage of business. Choose Etsy if: You are at the validation stage. You want to test whether your product sells without investing heavily upfront. You don’t want to worry about traffic yet, and your priority is getting initial sales quickly. Etsy works well if your product fits into categories where buyers are already searching, like handmade, personalized, or giftable items. Choose Shopify if: You are thinking beyond early sales. You want to build a brand, improve margins, and create a business that customers come back to directly. You’re willing to invest in marketing and want control over how your business grows. Shopify is the better choice if you’re planning to scale, expand product lines, or build long-term value. 💡 doola’s Advice The smartest approach is not choosing one over the other blindly. Start with Etsy to validate demand and understand what sells. Once you have traction, move to Shopify and make it your primary store. Use Etsy as a discovery channel, but build your brand and customer base on Shopify. How to Transition from Etsy to Shopify Moving from a marketplace to an independent storefront is a significant operational shift that requires a calculated, multi-phase approach. The most successful brands do not “leave” Etsy; they transition it from their primary storefront to a top-of-funnel discovery channel while building their long-term equity on Shopify. When To Transition The move to Shopify typically makes sense when the business shows consistent traction and operational clarity. Common indicators include: Monthly revenue consistently above $1,000–$5,000 A measurable share of repeat customers Increasing fee impact on margins due to Etsy’s transaction and advertising costs A need for stronger brand control and direct customer relationships At this stage, continuing solely on Etsy can limit growth efficiency. How To Migrate Operations The transition should begin with setting up Shopify as a parallel channel, not a replacement. A seamless transition ensures that your sales momentum remains uninterrupted. Here are the key steps: Data Transfer: Use the native CSV export tool in Etsy Shop Manager to download product listings, including titles, descriptions, and prices. For larger catalogs, 2026-standard migration apps like Matrixify or LitExtension can automate the transfer of product variants, images, and order history. Operational Parity: Before going live, ensure your Shopify shipping zones, tax settings, and payment gateways (Shopify Payments) mirror or improve upon your Etsy setup. Parallel Running: Do not shut down your Etsy shop. Maintain it as a secondary sales channel to capture marketplace search traffic while your Shopify SEO gains traction. Keep in mind: ✔️ Recreate your product catalog on Shopify (manually or via CSV import tools) ✔️ Set up payment gateways such as Shopify Payments or third-party providers ✔️ Configure shipping rules, taxes, and domain ✔️ Test the full purchase flow before directing any traffic It is important to keep the Etsy store active during this phase to avoid revenue disruption. Orders, inventory, and fulfillment processes should remain consistent across both platforms until Shopify stabilizes. How To Migrate Customers (Policy-Compliant) Etsy restricts the use of customer data for unsolicited off-platform marketing. This means you cannot directly export customer information and promote your Shopify store without consent. Instead, the customer transition should be gradual and compliant. Here are core things to keep in mind during the customer transition: Package Inserts: Include a high-quality physical card in every Etsy order. Offer a “First-Purchase Discount” or a “Loyalty Reward” exclusive to your Shopify URL. The “Around the Web” Section: Use the official link fields in your Etsy Shop Profile to point toward your Shopify store and social media channels. Banner Branding: Use your Etsy shop banner to display your independent domain name clearly, fostering brand recall without violating direct-linking policies in private messages. Building an Owned Audience The ultimate goal of the transition is the accumulation of first-party data . Unlike Etsy, Shopify allows you to build a customer database that you own entirely. To reduce long-term dependency on Etsy, here’s what you need to do: Email & SMS Capture: Implement a “welcome pop-up” on your Shopify store offering an immediate incentive (e.g., a free digital guide or 10% off) in exchange for an email address. Retention Marketing: Use automated email flows to reach out to customers on their birthdays or after 30 days of inactivity. This reduces your dependency on expensive ads and marketplace algorithms, turning one-time buyers into a self-sustaining revenue stream. Keep in mind: The transition from Etsy to Shopify should be gradual and structured. Etsy can continue to function as a discovery channel, while Shopify becomes the primary platform for brand building, customer retention, and long-term growth. Start Your E-Commerce Business The Right Way With doola Once you move beyond the initial Shopify vs Etsy confusion and decision, the next priority is building your business on the right legal and operational foundation. Getting sales is one part of growth. Structuring the business properly is what helps you sustain and scale it. To operate seriously, you need more than a storefront. You need the basics in place to support payments, compliance, and long-term expansion. Here are the three core components of a long-lasting business: Legal Business Structure: Forming an LLC or Corporation protects your personal assets from business-related liabilities and lawsuits. Tax Compliance: Accurate federal and state filings are mandatory to avoid significant IRS penalties and maintain your company’s “good standing.” Business Banking: Dedicated accounts are necessary to track margins accurately and integrate with professional payment processors. This is where doola fits in. We provide an integrated Business-in-a-Box™ solution designed specifically for modern business owners, including international entrepreneurs. Our platform is built to help entrepreneurs like you set up and manage some of these intricate backend requirements without needing to jump across multiple systems independently. By centralizing the administrative requirements, doola helps you: Form a U.S. LLC remotely, even if you are not based in the United States Stay compliant with ongoing tax and filing requirements Get support with setting up business bank accounts and integrated bookkeeping that syncs with platforms like Shopify Start your e-commerce business the right way with doola today. FAQs Is Shopify better than Etsy for beginners? It depends on your goal. Etsy is better for absolute beginners who want to start selling immediately with zero marketing experience, as it provides built-in customers. Shopify is better for beginners who are serious about building a standalone brand and are willing to learn how to drive their own traffic via social media or ads. Can I use Shopify and Etsy together? Yes, you can use Shopify and Etsy together and many successful sellers do. You can use Etsy as a discovery channel to find new customers and Shopify as your primary storefront where you keep higher margins. There are several apps available in 2026 that sync your inventory across both platforms automatically. Which platform is cheaper: Shopify or Etsy? Etsy is cheaper for low-volume sellers because it has no monthly subscription fee. However, Shopify becomes cheaper once you cross approximately $1,350 in monthly sales . At that point, Etsy’s 6.5% transaction fees usually exceed Shopify’s flat $39 monthly cost. Is Etsy good for long-term business growth? Etsy is excellent for consistent sales, but it has a “growth ceiling” due to its percentage-based fees and limited branding. For unlimited scaling and building a business you can eventually sell, Shopify is the superior long-term choice because you own the customer data and the platform Do I need an LLC to sell on Shopify or Etsy? You are not legally required to have an LLC to start . You can sell as a Sole Proprietor. However, as your sales grow, forming an LLC is highly recommended to protect your personal assets from business liabilities and to take advantage of professional tax benefits. Can I migrate my Etsy store to Shopify? Yes. You can export your product data into a CSV file from Etsy and import it directly into Shopify. For a more comprehensive transition (including reviews and customer history), professional migration tools like Matrixify are commonly used in 2026. Which platform is better for print-on-demand businesses? Shopify is generally better for POD because it offers deeper integrations with suppliers and allows for the high-profit margins needed to offset ad costs. While you can sell POD on Etsy, the marketplace is highly saturated, making it harder to stand out without a unique niche. The next chapter of your business starts with one call.
